briefing.headline: Set up the foundation. Once. Properly.
body: Your Mac shipped with Terminal.app and zsh. Terminal.app is fine — we're swapping it for iTerm2, which is better in every measurable way. zsh stays. What your Mac didn't ship with: Homebrew, the Mac package manager. Every developer tool you'll use installs through it.
This isn't a module. It's a prerequisite. Mostly waiting for installers. Do it once, do it right, never think about it again.

reference.title: Verify your setup
reference.content:
brew --version       # Homebrew is installed
git --version        # Git is installed
echo $SHELL          # Should return /bin/zsh

reference.title: Homebrew basics — you'll use these constantly
reference.content:
brew install <name>   Install a package
brew update           Update Homebrew itself
brew upgrade          Upgrade everything installed
brew list             See everything installed
brew doctor           Diagnose problems

reference.title: Where Homebrew lives
reference.content:
Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4): /opt/homebrew/bin/
Intel: /usr/local/bin/
If your Mac is from 2020 or later, you almost certainly have Apple Silicon.

reference.title: "command not found: brew"
reference.content: You're on Apple Silicon and didn't run the two PATH commands the installer printed (Step 4). Run them, then close and reopen iTerm2.

reference.title: "command not found: git" after brew install
reference.content: Close and reopen iTerm2. Shell needs to reload.

completion.headline: M0 complete.
completion.body: Your environment is ready. Next up: M1 — Terminal Fundamentals.

steps.title: Install iTerm2
steps.body: iTerm2 replaces Terminal.app. Better color, split panes, search, click-to-open URLs. Free. No account.
notes: Go to iterm2.com and click Download
Drag iTerm2 into your Applications folder
If macOS asks to confirm a downloaded app: click Open
steps.verify: iTerm2 is open. Close Terminal.app — you won't be using it again.

steps.title: Confirm iTerm2 works
steps.body: Type a command. If it prints back, you're in business.

steps.title: Install Homebrew
steps.body: The Mac package manager — the front door for installing nearly every developer tool you'll touch (Node, Git, Python, the AWS CLI, ffmpeg, dozens more). One command installs the thing. No App Store, no DMG drag-and-drop, no PATH spelunking. You'll run brew install <name> hundreds of times before this course is over.
steps.tryCue: Paste the whole thing as one line. Press Enter, then wait.
notes: macOS will ask for your password. Type it. Nothing appears as you type — that is normal. Press Enter.
If asked to install Xcode Command Line Tools: press Enter to confirm. Several minutes of waiting.
Wait for "==> Installation successful!" — the installer prints a lot of output. That is fine.
steps.verify: You see Installation successful! in the output.
whenYoullReachForThis: A tutorial says "first, install ffmpeg" — that's brew install ffmpeg, not a hunt for an installer
Claude Code tells you to install a CLI tool you don't have — Homebrew is almost always how
You set up a new Mac and want every dev tool back fast — install Homebrew first, then brew install the rest
Something you installed months ago is broken or outdated — brew upgrade <name> or brew reinstall <name>
You want to remove a tool cleanly without dotfiles scattered everywhere — brew uninstall <name>

steps.title: Configure Homebrew PATH
steps.body:
On Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4), Homebrew installs to /opt/homebrew/bin — which isn't on your PATH yet. PATH is the list of directories your shell searches when you type a command; if a directory isn't on PATH, anything inside it might as well not exist. The two lines below tell zsh where Homebrew lives, then apply that change to the current session.

Intel Macs: skip this step. The installer handles it.
steps.tryCue: Run both lines. Copy them exactly from your Homebrew output.

commandNotes.what: Appends a line to ~/.zprofile — a config file zsh runs every time it starts a new login shell.
commandNotes.when: Any tool's install instructions tell you to "add this line to your shell config so it loads every time." nvm, pyenv, conda, and Homebrew itself all use this pattern.

commandNotes.what: Runs the same PATH-setup the next zsh login would run — but in your current session, so you don't have to restart yet.
commandNotes.when: You just edited a shell config and want it to take effect now instead of opening a new terminal. The source ~/.zshrc idiom is the same trick for a different file.

steps.verify: Both commands run with no output and no errors.
whenYoullReachForThis: brew install succeeds but typing the new command gives "command not found" — PATH didn't pick it up
You install nvm or pyenv and the README tells you to add a line to ~/.zprofile or ~/.zshrc
Moving to a new Mac and your old terminal customizations are gone — they live in shell config files you can copy over
Claude Code says "add this to your shell" — it means a line like the ones above, in ~/.zprofile or ~/.zshrc

steps.title: Restart iTerm2
steps.body: Close iTerm2 completely (Cmd + Q) and reopen. This forces the shell to reload the new PATH settings.
steps.verify: iTerm2 is open in a fresh window.

steps.title: Verify Homebrew
steps.body: Confirm brew is installed and on your PATH.
steps.trouble: If "command not found: brew" — you skipped Step 4 or didn't restart iTerm2 in Step 5. Go back.

steps.title: Install Git
steps.body: Your Mac has a Git built in. It is old. Replace it with the Homebrew version — same command pattern you'll use for every other tool.
steps.tryCue: Run it. Wait for the install to finish.
steps.verify: Wait for the install to finish. No errors at the end.

steps.title: Verify Git
steps.body: Confirm the new Git is what runs when you type "git".

steps.title: Verify your shell is zsh
steps.body: Modern macOS defaults to zsh, but worth confirming before moving on. M1 covers shells in depth — for now, you just need to know which one you're in.
steps.trouble: If it returns bash: run chsh -s /bin/zsh and reopen iTerm2.

steps.title: Install Oh My Zsh
steps.body: A framework that makes your prompt more informative and adds shortcuts. Many devs use it. Skip if you want simplicity — you can come back any time.
steps.tryCue: Paste it. Wait for the prompt to change.
steps.verify: Your prompt looks different after restart. That's the point.
